name: Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System

clinicalPearls: A low serum testosterone with an elevated LH localizes the defect to the testis (primary/hypergonadotropic hypogonadism), whereas a low or inappropriately normal LH points to a hypothalamic-pituitary defect (secondary/hypogonadotropic hypogonadism) (p.3107, p.3118).

Acquired androgen-deficient men commonly report decreased libido, fewer sexual thoughts and acts, low energy, low mood, and (less often) hot flushes; eunuchoid body proportions (arm span >2 cm greater than height) indicate that deficiency predated epiphyseal fusion (p.3110).

Klinefelter syndrome (classically 47,XXY) is the most common chromosomal cause of testicular dysfunction and male infertility, occurring in about 1 in 600 live-born males, with markedly small testes (often 1-2 mL), azoospermia, low testosterone, raised estradiol, undervirilization, and gynecomastia (p.3110, p.3114).

True glandular gynecomastia (palpable firm, cord-like tissue >4 cm, often tender) reflects an increased estrogen-to-androgen ratio and must be distinguished from excess adipose (lipomastia); recent rapid onset, tenderness, or occurrence in a lean man warrants workup (p.3115).

Testicular volume is a useful clinical index: normal adult testes are 3.5-5.5 cm long (about 12-25 mL by Prader orchidometer), and very small testes in a hypogonadal man should prompt a karyotype to exclude Klinefelter syndrome (p.3110, p.3119).

Mumps is the classic cause of viral orchitis; orchitis develops in up to one-fourth of affected adult men, is unilateral in about two-thirds, and semen analysis normalizes in three-fourths after unilateral but only one-third after bilateral involvement (p.3114).

Total testosterone can mislead when SHBG is altered (low in obesity, diabetes, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome; high in aging, hyperthyroidism, estrogen, HIV/hepatitis B and C, some anticonvulsants); measure free testosterone (ideally by equilibrium dialysis) in these settings (p.3106, p.3108).

Cryptorchidism, even when corrected before puberty, carries increased risk of malignancy, infertility, inguinal hernia, and torsion, and is considered part of the testicular dysgenesis syndrome along with hypospadias, impaired spermatogenesis, and testicular cancer (p.3114).
Selective elevation of FSH (with relatively normal LH) suggests seminiferous tubule/Sertoli cell damage, because reduced inhibin B removes the negative feedback restraining FSH (p.3104, p.3107).
Up to two-thirds of pubertal boys and about half of hospitalized men have benign palpable breast tissue, so not all gynecomastia requires extensive investigation (p.3116).

Kallmann syndrome is the anosmic form of congenital GnRH-deficient hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, arising from defective olfactory bulb morphogenesis and failed migration of GnRH neurons; micropenis and a history of cryptorchidism favor a congenital central defect over self-limited delayed puberty (p.3112, p.3110).
harrison.pathophysiology: The hypothalamic-pituitary-testicular axis governs androgen production and spermatogenesis. Pulsatile hypothalamic GnRH (regulated by kisspeptin, neurokinin B, and dynorphin in KNDy neurons) drives pituitary LH and FSH roughly every 1-3 h. LH stimulates Leydig cell testosterone synthesis (rate-limited by StAR-mediated cholesterol transport into mitochondria and CYP11A1 side-chain cleavage); FSH acts on Sertoli cells to support spermatogenesis and inhibin B production, the latter selectively suppressing FSH. Testosterone is converted by 5-alpha-reductase (SRD5A2) to the more potent DHT (required for external genital virilization and prostate growth) and aromatized by CYP19 to estradiol (mediating effects on bone, epiphyseal closure, libido). Disorders arise from gonadotropin deficiency (secondary/hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, congenital such as GnRH-deficient/Kallmann syndrome or acquired from sellar masses, hyperprolactinemia, hemochromatosis, illness, drugs, obesity) or primary testicular failure (hypergonadotropic), e.g., Klinefelter syndrome, cryptorchidism, orchitis, chemo/radiation, torsion. Resistance syndromes (androgen receptor mutations, 5-alpha-reductase or aromatase deficiency) impair androgen action or conversion. Gynecomastia results from a relative excess of estrogen action on breast tissue (p.3102-3116).
additionalDifferentials: Erectile dysfunction without testosterone deficiency (the two are distinct disorders that may coexist)
Self-limited (constitutional) delayed puberty versus congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism in adolescents
Sellar mass lesions / pituitary adenoma impairing gonadotropin secretion
Functional hypogonadotropic hypogonadism from systemic illness, malnutrition, eating disorders, or opioid use
infectionMimics: Mumps orchitis (and orchitis from echovirus, lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus, group B arboviruses) causing acquired primary testicular failure
HIV infection associated with low testosterone (primary or central)
Lepromatous leprosy causing testicular atrophy through direct mycobacterial invasion
nonInfectiousMimics: Age-related decline in testosterone overlapping with symptomatic hypogonadism
Obesity-related lowering of total testosterone (with often normal free testosterone) due to reduced SHBG

Free testosterone by equilibrium dialysis when SHBG is altered (aging, obesity, chronic illness)
LH and FSH to separate primary (high LH/FSH) from secondary (low/inappropriately normal LH) hypogonadism
Karyotype in men with low testosterone, elevated LH, and small testes to diagnose Klinefelter syndrome
Serum prolactin and ferritin/transferrin saturation; pituitary MRI when secondary hypogonadism is found
Inhibin B (Sertoli cell product) to assess seminiferous tubule integrity
Semen analysis and Y-chromosome microdeletion testing (AZFa/AZFb/AZFc) in oligo-/azoospermia
For gynecomastia: testosterone, estradiol, estrone, androstenedione, LH, hCG (beta), TSH; testicular ultrasound and adrenal/chest imaging if an estrogen- or hCG-secreting tumor is suspected

Markedly elevated estradiol with suppressed LH, suggesting a testicular or adrenal estrogen-secreting tumor
Elevated hCG (beta) prompting search for an hCG-producing germ cell or other tumor
Very small testes with low testosterone and high LH (consider Klinefelter syndrome and its associated breast cancer risk)
Diabetes insipidus accompanying hypogonadism, suggesting craniopharyngioma or infiltrative hypothalamic lesion
Hyperprolactinemia with visual field defects suggesting a pituitary mass
harrison.prognosis: Outcomes depend on the underlying disorder. Secondary (hypogonadotropic) hypogonadism is highly amenable to fertility restoration with pulsatile GnRH or gonadotropins, and 10-20% of congenital GnRH-deficient men may have spontaneous reversal in adulthood. In Klinefelter syndrome azoospermia is the rule, though sperm can sometimes be retrieved surgically (including in some non-mosaic men) for ICSI. After mumps orchitis the testis may recover or atrophy. Radiation effects on spermatogenesis are dose-dependent (transient decline below 1 Gy, temporary azoospermia at 1-2 Gy, usually permanent azoospermia above 2 Gy), while Leydig cells are relatively radioresistant (dysfunction generally only above 20 Gy). The age-related testosterone decline is gradual and progressive without a discrete abrupt fall (p.3107, p.3114-3115, p.3117).
pitfalls: Relying on a single random or afternoon testosterone level — values are pulsatile, diurnal, lower in the late afternoon and after meals, and depressed by acute illness, so confirm with a fasting early-morning sample (p.3108, p.3118).
Interpreting total testosterone without accounting for SHBG changes, leading to over- or under-diagnosis in obesity, aging, thyroid disease, or chronic illness (p.3106, p.3108).
Mislabeling the normal aging decline as 'andropause' — there is no discrete andropause and population screening of all older men is not recommended (p.3117).
Subjecting every man with gynecomastia to extensive workup, when most pubertal and many hospitalized men have benign glandular tissue (p.3116).
Confusing retractile testis (no treatment needed) with true cryptorchidism (p.3114).
Assuming corrected unilateral cryptorchidism guarantees normal fertility — sperm counts can remain reduced (p.3114).
Overlooking drug, alcohol, opioid, marijuana, or anabolic-androgenic steroid use as reversible causes of suppressed testosterone (p.3114, p.3119).
harrison.severityClassification: Diagnostic stratification of male testosterone deficiency (Harrison Fig. 403-8): early-morning total testosterone >350-400 ng/dL makes androgen deficiency unlikely; borderline values 200-350 ng/dL should be repeated with free testosterone; consistently low levels (notably <200 ng/dL) in association with symptoms confirm deficiency. Localization: high LH/FSH = primary (hypergonadotropic) testicular failure; low/inappropriately normal LH = secondary (hypogonadotropic). Harmonized normal total testosterone reference range in healthy young men is 264-916 ng/dL (p.3108, p.3117-3118).
management: Testosterone replacement therapy (by gel or injection) is the mainstay for symptomatic androgen deficiency in primary or secondary hypogonadism
For fertility in secondary (hypogonadotropic) hypogonadism use gonadotropin therapy or pulsatile GnRH to induce spermatogenesis, avoiding exogenous testosterone which suppresses it
Treat reversible causes by correcting hyperprolactinaemia with a dopamine agonist, managing iron overload in haemochromatosis, and withdrawing offending drugs
Monitor men on testosterone replacement with haematocrit, prostate-specific antigen, and bone density
Offer assisted reproduction with testicular sperm extraction and intracytoplasmic sperm injection for azoospermia, as in Klinefelter syndrome
Manage true glandular gynaecomastia by treating the cause and considering an antioestrogen or surgery for persistent tissue
Obtain a karyotype and provide genetic counselling where a chromosomal cause such as Klinefelter syndrome is identified
Refer to endocrinology, andrology, and fertility services
